ref: DAR — Revelation ch. 10: The Proclamation of the Advent
title: The Proclamation of the Advent
voicePrompt: In your own words, explain Smith's argument that the angel's little book is the prophecy of Daniel, that 'time shall be no longer' means prophetic time ending in 1844, and how the eating of the book pictures the joy and bitter disappointment of the Advent movement.

questions.stem: Why does Smith call chapter 10 a 'parenthetical prophecy'?
options: Because it repeats events already described under the sixth trumpet
Because it comes in between the sounding of the sixth trumpet and the seventh, which is not introduced until chapter 11:15
Because it was added later and is not part of John's original vision
Because it describes events that never actually came to pass
questions.explanation: Smith explains that chapter 9 closed with the sixth trumpet, and the seventh is not introduced until 11:15; therefore all of chapter 10 and part of chapter 11 come in parenthetically between the sixth and seventh trumpets.

questions.stem: What does Smith conclude the 'little book' open in the angel's hand actually is?
options: The book of Revelation itself
The gospel of John
The book of the prophecy of Daniel, which had been shut up and sealed until the time of the end
A new book never before seen in Scripture
questions.explanation: Smith argues that the only book described as closed up and sealed is Daniel's prophecy (Daniel 12:4), that both books deal with time, and so the little book the angel holds open is the book of Daniel, now unsealed at the time of the end.

questions.stem: According to Smith, when did the 'time of the end' commence and the little book become opened?
options: In A.D. 538, when papal supremacy began
In A.D. 1798, when the 1260 years of papal rule expired
In A.D. 1844, at the close of the prophetic periods
At the destruction of Jerusalem in A.D. 70
questions.explanation: Smith says the supremacy of the little horn reached to the time of the end and ended in A.D. 1798, where the 1260 years of papal rule expired; there the time of the end commenced and the book was opened, after which knowledge of the prophecies greatly increased.

questions.stem: How does Smith identify the angel of Revelation 10 with the first angel of Revelation 14?
options: Both angels carry the same little book in their hands
Both have a special message, cry with a loud voice, refer to the Creator of heaven, earth, and sea, and proclaim time
Both are named explicitly in the text as Gabriel
Both appear in the same verse of chapter 14
questions.explanation: Smith lists four points of identity: both have a special message, both utter it with a loud voice, both refer to the great Creator as maker of heaven, earth, and sea, and both proclaim time — one swearing time should be no more, the other proclaiming the hour of God's Judgment is come.

questions.stem: What does Smith conclude the declaration 'time shall be no longer' must mean?
options: That literal time in this world ends at the angel's message
That probationary time closes immediately
That prophetic time ends — no prophetic period would extend beyond this message
That the seventh trumpet would never sound
questions.explanation: Smith reasons it cannot mean literal time (the seventh angel's days are still future) nor probationary time (which continues until Christ ends His priestly work); it must therefore mean prophetic time, since the longest prophetic periods all close, ending in the autumn of 1844.

questions.stem: What does Smith say the 'mystery of God' that is to be finished refers to?
options: The seven thunders, which were sealed up
The secret meaning of the prophetic numbers
The gospel, which will be finished when the number of God's people is made up and probation closes
The restoration of the Jewish temple
questions.explanation: Drawing on Ephesians and Galatians, Smith concludes the mystery of God is the gospel; its finishing is the close of the work of taking out from the nations a people for God's name, when mercy ceases to be offered and probation closes.

questions.stem: How does Smith interpret John eating the little book that was sweet in his mouth but bitter in his belly?
options: As a warning against studying prophecy too eagerly
As the joy of receiving the message of Christ's immediate coming, followed by the bitter disappointment when the Lord did not come in 1844
As the contrast between the Old and New Testaments
As John's literal sickness during his exile on Patmos
questions.explanation: Smith says many living met a striking fulfillment in the honey-like sweetness of the truths of Christ's immediate coming, followed by the sadness when the Lord did not come in 1844; those who endured learned the mistake was only in the event, not in the time.

questions.stem: What does Smith say the final commission in verse 11 — 'Thou must prophesy again before many peoples, and nations, and tongues, and kings' — foretells?
options: A return to preaching the first and second angels' messages
The third angel's message, going forth after the first and second messages ceased
The rebuilding of the church at Ephesus
John's personal release from the island of Patmos
questions.explanation: Smith reads this as a prophecy of the third angel's message, given to John as representative of the church, to go forth after the first and second messages ceased — and not done in a corner, but before many peoples, nations, tongues, and kings.
